lead: A Markov chain moves probabilities from state to state. A steady-state distribution is a probability vector π that the transition matrix leaves unchanged: after one step the distribution is still π. A limiting distribution is the long-run distribution that p<sub>n</sub> approaches as n grows. For a finite, irreducible, aperiodic chain the two coincide and are unique. Engineers use this to predict long-run load, failure rates, queue occupancy, and weather-like repeated experiments without simulating every step.
prereq: You need: transition matrices and state classification from 7.4, and probability vectors from Unit 2, Probability and Random Variables.

blocks.text: Let p<sub>n</sub> be a row vector. Its i-th entry is the probability that the chain is in state i after n steps. Let P be the one-step transition matrix; P<sub>ij</sub> is the probability of moving from i to j in one step. The chain updates by p<sub>n+1</sub> = p<sub>n</sub>P. A stationary distribution is a row vector π with non-negative entries that sum to 1 and satisfies π = πP. If the chain starts with distribution π, then every later distribution is also π. The chain's probability mass is balanced: the flow into each state equals the flow out.

blocks.where: π is a row probability vector; P is the transition matrix; π<sub>i</sub> is the long-run fraction of time in state i under the conditions in the next section.

blocks.text: For a finite, irreducible, aperiodic chain, exactly one such π exists. Irreducible means every state can reach every other state. Aperiodic means the chain is not forced to return only at times that are multiples of some period greater than 1. Some syllabi call π the equilibrium distribution or the invariant distribution. It is not generally the vector of one-step transition probabilities, and it is not the same as the initial distribution.

The limiting distribution is the vector lim<sub>n→∞</sub> p<sub>n</sub>, when this limit exists and does not depend on the starting distribution. For a finite irreducible aperiodic chain, the limit exists and equals the unique stationary π. Then π<sub>i</sub> is also the long-run fraction of steps spent in state i.

Periodicity breaks the equality. Take P = [[0,1],[1,0]]. The stationary distribution is π = (1/2,1/2). If p<sub>0</sub> = (1,0), then p<sub>1</sub> = (0,1), p<sub>2</sub> = (1,0), and so on. The sequence has no limit, although π is stationary. Reducibility also breaks uniqueness: a chain with two separate closed classes can have many stationary distributions.

The mean recurrence time m<sub>i</sub> is the expected number of steps between two successive visits to state i, including the return step. For an irreducible positive recurrent chain, m<sub>i</sub> = 1/π<sub>i</sub>. A large π<sub>i</sub> means state i is common and returns quickly; a small π<sub>i</sub> means it is rare and returns slowly.

Write the unknown row vector π = (π<sub>1</sub>,...,π<sub>k</sub>). The matrix equation π = πP gives k scalar equations. One equation is redundant because the rows of P sum to 1. Replace any one equation with the normalisation Σπ<sub>i</sub>=1, then solve the remaining linear system. Check every π<sub>i</sub> ≥ 0.

items: Write π = πP as π(I − P) = 0, where I is the identity matrix.

blocks.text: For two states with P = [[1−a, a],[b, 1−b]], where a is the probability of leaving state 1 and b is the probability of leaving state 2, the stationary distribution is π = (b/(a+b), a/(a+b)) when a+b > 0. This shortcut comes from π<sub>1</sub>(1−a)+π<sub>2</sub>b = π<sub>1</sub>, which simplifies to aπ<sub>1</sub> = bπ<sub>2</sub>. The same equation plus π<sub>1</sub>+π<sub>2</sub>=1 gives the result.

figure.caption: The sunny probability starts at 1 on day 0, drops at day 1, and settles towards 0.6; the gap from 0.6 halves each step.

spec.aria: A plot of sunny probability against step number rises from 1 and settles towards 0.6.

examples.question: Days in a city are either Sunny (S) or Rainy (R). The one-step transition matrix is P = [[0.8,0.2],[0.3,0.7]], with rows S and R. On day 0 it is Sunny, so p<sub>0</sub> = (1,0). Find the stationary distribution π. Find p<sub>n</sub>(S), the probability of Sun on day n, and its limit. Find the mean recurrence times of S and R in days.
steps: Let π = (π<sub>S</sub>, π<sub>R</sub>). The equation π = πP gives π<sub>S</sub> = 0.8π<sub>S</sub> + 0.3π<sub>R</sub>, π<sub>R</sub> = 0.2π<sub>S</sub> + 0.7π<sub>R</sub>.
The first equation gives 0.2π<sub>S</sub> = 0.3π<sub>R</sub>, so π<sub>S</sub> = 1.5π<sub>R</sub>.
Add the normalisation π<sub>S</sub>+π<sub>R</sub>=1. Substitute: 1.5π<sub>R</sub>+π<sub>R</sub>=1, so 2.5π<sub>R</sub>=1, π<sub>R</sub>=0.4.

For this two-state chain a=0.2 and b=0.3. The second eigenvalue is 1−a−b=0.5. Hence p<sub>n</sub>(S)=π<sub>S</sub>+(p<sub>0</sub>(S)−π<sub>S</sub>)(0.5)<sup>n</sup> = 0.6+(1−0.6)(0.5)<sup>n</sup> = 0.6+0.4(0.5)<sup>n</sup>.
Check n=0: 0.6+0.4=1. Check n=1: 0.6+0.2=0.8, which equals P<sub>SS</sub>=0.8.
As n→∞, (0.5)<sup>n</sup>→0, so the limit is 0.6.
Mean recurrence time of S is 1/π<sub>S</sub>=1/0.6=1.6666666666666667 days. For R it is 1/0.4=2.5 days.
examples.answer: π=(0.6,0.4); p<sub>n</sub>(S)=0.6+0.4(0.5)<sup>n</sup>; the limiting probability of Sun is 0.6; the mean recurrence times are 1.6666666666666667 days for Sunny and 2.5 days for Rainy.
examples.check:
piS = 0.3 / (0.2 + 0.3)
piR = 0.2 / (0.2 + 0.3)
mS = 1 / piS
mR = 1 / piR
print(piS)
print(piR)
print(mS)
print(mR)

traps: A stationary distribution can exist while the limit does not: P=[[0,1],[1,0]] has π=(1/2,1/2), but p<sub>n</sub> alternates from (1,0).
Do not omit Σπ<sub>i</sub>=1. The equation π=πP alone leaves any multiple of π as a solution.
For a reducible chain, stationary distributions are not unique. The long-run fraction can depend on the starting state.
Use row vectors with π=πP for the convention in this chapter. Writing Pπ=π with column vectors is also valid, but mixing the two transposes the matrix.
Mean recurrence time is 1/π<sub>i</sub>, not π<sub>i</sub>. If π<sub>i</sub>=0.2, the mean return is 5 steps, not 0.2.

quiz.q: Define a stationary distribution of a Markov chain with transition matrix P.
quiz.a: A row probability vector π with π=πP, Σπ<sub>i</sub>=1, and π<sub>i</sub>≥0 for every state i.

quiz.q: Why does a finite irreducible aperiodic chain have a unique stationary distribution that is also the limit?
quiz.a: Irreducibility gives one communicating class; aperiodicity removes cyclic alternation; finiteness gives positive recurrence. Hence one π exists and p<sub>n</sub>→π from every starting distribution.

quiz.q: P=[[0,1],[1,0]], p<sub>0</sub>=(1,0). Does a limiting distribution exist? Does a stationary distribution exist?
quiz.a: A stationary distribution exists: π=(0.5,0.5). The limiting distribution does not exist because p<sub>n</sub> alternates between (1,0) and (0,1).

quiz.q: If π=(0.25,0.75), find the mean recurrence times of the two states.
What goes wrong if you solve π=πP without the sum-to-one condition?
quiz.a: The equations are homogeneous, so any scalar multiple of a solution is also a solution. The sum-to-one condition fixes the scale and makes π a probability vector.

quiz.q: A chain has two closed classes with stationary distributions π<sub>A</sub> and π<sub>B</sub>. What long-run distributions are possible from a mixed start?
quiz.a: Any convex combination λπ<sub>A</sub>+(1−λ)π<sub>B</sub> with 0≤λ≤1, where λ is the probability mass that ends in class A. The long-run distribution is not unique without more information.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same fixed-point idea powers PageRank, where a random surfer's stationary distribution ranks web pages. Markov chain Monte Carlo uses a chain built to have a chosen stationary distribution and samples from it. Queueing and reliability models read long-run congestion and failure rates from π. Search for “stationary distribution PageRank”, “Markov chain Monte Carlo”, and “mean recurrence time”.
